significance: Anthropic's current top-tier release, aimed at heavy-duty agentic coding and extended reasoning tasks, ships with adaptive thinking on by default (it can't be switched off) and a 1M-token context window out of the box. It became generally available on June 9, 2026 across the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry, alongside a Project-Glasswing-restricted sibling, Claude Mythos 5. Anthropic's own models-overview guidance now directs developers who need the ceiling of available capability toward Fable 5 rather than Opus 4.8 -- a signal that Fable 5, not Opus 4.8, now sits atop Anthropic's publicly available lineup.

Claude Opus 5, released July 24, 2026, slots between Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 in Anthropic's own pricing table ($5/$25 per million input/output tokens, versus Fable 5's $10/$50 and Sonnet 5's $3/$15) -- Anthropic's own announcement frames it as coming close to Fable 5's frontier intelligence at half the price. It carries the same 1M-token context window and 128k max output as the rest of the current generation. Opus 4.8, the prior Opus-branded flagship, now sits in Anthropic's own docs under a "Legacy models" heading.

Claude Sonnet 5, released June 30, 2026, is Anthropic's mid-tier model in the current generation -- same 1M-token context window and 128k max output as Fable 5 and Opus 5, at $3/$15 per million input/output tokens (an introductory $2/$10 runs through August 31, 2026). Anthropic's own current-focus messaging positions it as narrowing the capability gap to the Opus-class flagship at a lower price.

DeepSeek's newest flagship reasoning and agentic model extends default context to 1 million tokens and, per Lab DeepSeek, approaches the performance of leading closed frontier models while remaining open-weight and far cheaper to run via API.

DeepSeek-V4 Flash is the lighter sibling released alongside V4 Pro on the same day: a 284-billion-parameter (13 billion active) model that, per DeepSeek's own release notes, shares the same 1-million-token default context now standard across the company's official services, at a smaller active-parameter footprint than Pro.

Ai2 describes Olmo 3.1 -- an extended reinforcement-learning follow-up to the Olmo 3 family it first shipped on Nov 20, 2025 -- as its best-performing fully open 32B checkpoints to date for both reasoning (Think) and instruction-following (Instruct) use, citing internal evaluation gains over the original Olmo 3 32B models of over 5 points on AIME and over 20 points on IFBench.

Olmo Hybrid, released March 5, 2026, ships alongside (not replacing) the Olmo 3 line: a 7-billion-parameter model interleaving standard transformer attention with Gated DeltaNet linear-RNN layers at a 3:1 ratio. Ai2's own post reports "the hybrid model reaches the same accuracy as Olmo 3 using 49% fewer tokens" on MMLU, and its model card lists the same 65,536-token context window as the Olmo 3 family.

NVIDIA's newest and largest Nemotron 3 release, Ultra is a 550-billion-parameter (55 billion active) Mixture-of-Experts hybrid Mamba-Attention model built for long-running agentic workloads. NVIDIA's own benchmarks put its inference throughput at 1.6x to 5.9x that of three other open models (GLM-5.1-754B-A40B, Kimi-K2.6-1T-A32B, and Qwen-3.5-397B-17B), varying by which one it's measured against, at matching accuracy, plus strong long-context retrieval at its 1M-token window.

Nemotron 3 Nano, NVIDIA's smallest Nemotron 3 tier (30 billion total parameters, up to 3 billion active), launched Dec 15, 2025 as what NVIDIA calls "the most efficient family of open models with leading accuracy for building agentic AI" -- the entry point below Super and Ultra, sharing the same 1M-token context window.

Nemotron 3 Super, the mid tier between Nano and Ultra at 120 billion total parameters (12 billion active), released March 11, 2026 with the same 1M-token context window as its siblings. NVIDIA reports it delivers "up to 5x higher throughput and up to 2x higher accuracy" than the previous-generation Nemotron Super model.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, released April 28, 2026, is a 30B-A3B hybrid Mixture-of-Experts model built for multimodal agents -- accepting text, images, audio, video, and documents in, producing text out, on a 256,000-token context window. NVIDIA reports it delivers "9x higher throughput than other open omni models" at the same interactivity.

OpenAI began a limited preview of its GPT-5.6 family on June 26, 2026, led by Sol, the line's new flagship, alongside the mid-tier Terra and the fast, low-cost Luna. Per OpenAI's own preview system card, Sol pushes coding, biology, and cybersecurity capability further than any prior OpenAI release and adds new "max"/"ultra" reasoning and multi-subagent modes for long, complex problems, alongside a hardened safety stack with activation-classifier monitoring. OpenAI initially limited the preview to a small group of trusted partners coordinated with the U.S. government; that restriction lifted on July 9, 2026, when all three variants -- Sol, Terra, and Luna -- reached general availability across ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI API.

Terra is the GPT-5.6 family's mid-tier model, entering the same limited preview as flagship Sol on June 26, 2026 and reaching general availability alongside it on July 9, 2026 across ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI API. OpenAI prices it at $2.50/$15 per million input/output tokens, well below Sol, for teams that don't need the flagship's full capability.

Luna is the GPT-5.6 family's fast, low-cost model, entering the same limited preview as flagship Sol on June 26, 2026 and reaching general availability alongside it on July 9, 2026 across ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI API. OpenAI prices it at $1/$6 per million input/output tokens, the cheapest of the three variants.

GPT-Live-1, released July 8, 2026, is OpenAI's new full-duplex voice model -- OpenAI's own deployment-safety documentation says it and its mini sibling "can listen and respond continuously" rather than waiting for a clearly defined turn to end. It's the default voice experience for ChatGPT Go, Plus, and Pro; API access was announced without a firm date.

GPT-Live-1 mini, released the same day as GPT-Live-1, is the free-tier version of OpenAI's new full-duplex voice model line -- ChatGPT's free tier gets this model by default rather than the full GPT-Live-1.

Gemini 3.5 Flash, released May 19, 2026 as the first model in Google's new 3.5 family, is built for agentic workflows and coding rather than general chat; Google's own benchmark table has it outperforming Gemini 3.1 Pro on coding and multi-step agentic tasks while running roughly four times faster on output tokens per second than prior frontier models. It shipped broadly at once across the free Gemini app and Search's AI Mode, the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Android Studio, the new Antigravity developer platform, and Gemini Enterprise. A larger 3.5 Pro sibling remains in development. Google DeepMind is itself headquartered in London, UK -- a distinct entity from Google/Alphabet's Mountain View corporate HQ -- but this Board, per this project's own logged taxonomy decision, buckets it into the US section alongside its US-headquartered parent, since the Board's three tracked lanes are US, China, and notable open-weights releases, not a geography-complete list of every lab's home country.

Gemini 3.6 Flash, released July 21, 2026 alongside two siblings (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and a governments/trusted-partners-only Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber this Board cannot list under its own access-tier categories), takes over as Google's main workhorse tier from Gemini 3.5 Flash. It handles a 1M-token input context with a 64,000-token max output, across text, image, audio, and video input.
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, released the same day as Gemini 3.6 Flash, is Google's cheapest current-generation Gemini tier, positioned for high-volume, cost-sensitive use rather than maximum capability.

Muse Spark, unveiled April 8, 2026, is the first model in a new series built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, capping a nine-month, ground-up rebuild of Meta's AI stack, and is built to reason over text, images, and live camera or video input while answering in text, images, or code. It is rolling out primarily through consumer surfaces -- the Meta AI app, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, and Ray-Ban Meta glasses -- with only a private API preview open to select partners so far rather than a broad developer API. Meta says it hopes to open-source future Muse-series models, though Spark itself remains proprietary.

Muse Spark 1.1, released July 9, 2026, is Meta Superintelligence Labs' second release, adding gains in tool use, computer use, coding, and multimodal understanding over the original April Muse Spark. Unlike Muse Spark's private-partner-only preview, developers can now build with it directly via the new Meta Model API, now in public preview, and the model can actively manage a working context of 1 million tokens across a long agentic session. It also ships in "Thinking" mode in the Meta AI app and on meta.ai.

Grok 4.5, released July 8, 2026, is the first model shipped under the SpaceXAI brand following xAI's merger into SpaceX, and xAI's own developer documentation positions it as the company's most capable and fastest model yet, built for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work rather than general chat. It was trained jointly with Cursor -- incorporating a large volume of Cursor's real-world coding and agent-interaction data -- carries a 500,000-token context window, and is priced at $2/$6 per million input/output tokens. Elon Musk described it as "an Opus-class model, but faster, more token-efficient and lower cost," positioning it as a cheaper rival to Anthropic's and OpenAI's flagship models.

Mistral Large 3, released December 2, 2025, is Mistral's flagship sparse mixture-of-experts model -- 675 billion total parameters with 41 billion active per token -- released fully open under the Apache 2.0 license alongside the smaller Ministral 3 family (14B/8B/3B). It adds image understanding on top of text, supports 40-plus languages, and Mistral's own announcement places it at #2 among open-weight non-reasoning models on the LMArena leaderboard at launch. Mistral is headquartered in the EU, not the US, but this Board -- per this project's own logged taxonomy decision -- buckets it into the US section rather than a third regional column, since the Board's three tracked lanes are US, China, and notable open-weights releases, not a geography-complete list of every lab's home country.

Ministral 3, released the same day as flagship Mistral Large 3, is a smaller sibling family in three sizes (3B, 8B, 14B parameters), each with native image understanding alongside text, released fully open under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Mistral Medium 3.5 sits between Ministral 3 and flagship Large 3 in Mistral's lineup: a 128-billion-parameter dense model accepting text and image input with text output, on a 256,000-token context window, released open-weight under a Modified MIT license alongside parallel API pricing ($1.5/$7.5 per million input/output tokens).

Qwen3.7-Max, unveiled by Alibaba Cloud on May 21, 2026, is Alibaba's coding- and office-agent flagship, demonstrating sustained end-to-end autonomy across a 35-hour kernel-optimization run involving more than 1,000 tool calls with no manual intervention. It ships with a 1-million-token context window, OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs, and cross-framework support (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Qwen Code), available as a closed, proprietary API through Alibaba Cloud Model Studio rather than as downloadable weights.

Kimi K2.6, which Moonshot AI shipped as generally available around April 20, 2026, is a trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (32 billion active per token) built around long-horizon endurance rather than one-shot reasoning: its "Agent Swarm" system coordinates up to 300 sub-agents across roughly 4,000 steps in a single autonomous run, and it can sustain coding sessions for hours at a stretch. It is released open-weight on Hugging Face under a Modified MIT license, with a 256,000-token context window and multimodal (text, image, video) input support, and is also served through Kimi.com, the Kimi app, and Moonshot's own API and CLI.

Kimi K3, which Moonshot announced July 16, 2026, is a 2.8-trillion-parameter model built on Moonshot's own Kimi Delta Attention architecture, with native vision and a 1-million-token context window -- SCMP calls it "the world's largest open-source artificial intelligence model," though the open-weight release itself is still pending: Moonshot's own blog states "the full model weights will be released by July 27, 2026," and no Kimi-K3 repository exists on its Hugging Face org yet. Served today via kimi.com, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and Moonshot's API at $0.30-$15 per million tokens.

GLM-5.2, which Zhipu AI (Z.ai) released on June 17, 2026, refines the GLM-5 line for long-horizon coding and agentic work on a 1-million-token context window, using a new "IndexShare" sparse-attention mechanism that Zhipu's own model card says cuts per-token compute at that context length by roughly 2.9x. The roughly 753-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model is released open-weight under the MIT license -- no usage or regional restrictions -- through Hugging Face and Zhipu's own GLM Coding Plan and API, positioned as a coding-first engine rather than a general-purpose chat assistant.

Seed 2.1, which ByteDance's Seed team released on June 23, 2026 in Pro and lighter Turbo variants, is built to carry out full multi-step tasks -- project planning, document processing, end-to-end coding across an entire codebase -- rather than answer single prompts, and adds stronger multimodal understanding of documents, charts, and video. ByteDance serves it through its own Doubao consumer assistant and the Volcano Engine cloud platform rather than as downloadable weights or a widely available third-party API.

Seed 2.1 Turbo is the lighter, faster sibling ByteDance released alongside Seed 2.1 Pro on the same day. ByteDance's own model page confirms it as one of "two AI productivity models in different sizes: Pro and Turbo," backed by a 25-plus-benchmark comparison table -- the same page the original Pro citation predates and doesn't itself mention Turbo by name.
